opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, in hindsight, we were way too early. When Alexander and I left Google in 2017 to start NEAR as an AI company, the idea was program synthesis: teaching machines to write code from natural language descriptions. We'd just come off the Transformer work, and I was seeing how fast things were moving, so it felt like this was the next frontier.

But the reality was that the models at the time just weren't there. We were working with relatively small architectures, and the biggest bottleneck was data. To really teach a model to code, you need enormous amounts of paired examples, descriptions of what you want and the code that does it, and that simply didn't exist in a clean form. So we were trying to generate training data ourselves. We actually had crowdsourced workers, a lot of them students around the world, writing small programs and descriptions for us.

And that's actually where things took an unexpected turn. Paying those people was really hard. They were in places like China, Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia, and sending small amounts of money across borders was slow, expensive, and sometimes just impossible. We started looking at blockchain as a way to solve that payments problem, and found that the existing infrastructure couldn't handle what we needed. That's what led us to pivot and build NEAR Protocol.

So in terms of feasibility: the vision was right, the direction was right, but the timing was off by a few years. What we've seen since, with large language models trained on huge code corpora, scaling up compute, is essentially that vision coming true. It just needed the scale of data and compute that came later. And now, interestingly, the two threads are coming back together, with AI agents needing ownership, payments, and verifiable infrastructure, which is a big part of what we think about at NEAR today.

r001.rationale: The response says the models were small and data was the biggest bottleneck; it does not attribute the infeasibility to insufficient compute.

r002.rationale: It mentions students around the world writing programs and descriptions, but does not identify them as computer science students in developing countries or as a low-cost source.

r003.rationale: It describes crowdsourced workers writing small programs and descriptions for the training data, and says they were paid.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in hindsight, we were way too early. When Alex and I left Google, the idea was pretty straightforward on paper: take a natural language description and have a model produce working code. We'd been working on Transformer-based models, we understood sequence-to-sequence, and the leap from translating English to French to translating English to Python seemed, if not trivial, at least tractable.

The thing we underestimated wasn't the modeling. It was the data. There was no large, high-quality dataset of paired natural language and code at the scale you needed. Public repositories had code, but almost none of it had a faithful specification of what the code was supposed to do. Commit messages are not specs. Docstrings are often wrong or missing. So we ended up spending a huge amount of effort building a pipeline to collect that data. We had people writing small programs and describing them, we were trying crowdsourcing, we were looking at ways to pay developers around the world to produce labeled examples.

And that's actually what pulled us into blockchain, somewhat accidentally. We were trying to pay contributors in places like China and Eastern Europe, and the payment rails were terrible. Fees were high, transfers took days, some people couldn't receive money at all. We looked at crypto as a payments layer and realized the existing systems were unusable for that purpose. That's what became NEAR.

So, feasibility. The core bet turned out to be right. Models can learn to code, and today you see it everywhere. But what made it work was scale we didn't have access to in 2017, both in compute and in the sheer volume of code and text that the big labs could ingest a few years later. We were trying to do with a small team and curated data what ultimately got solved with orders of magnitude more parameters and basically the whole internet. I don't think we were wrong about the direction. We were wrong about how much brute force the problem would require, and we were a startup that couldn't afford the brute force.

r001.rationale: It says the team lacked the compute scale available later and that this was part of what the effort required in 2017.

r002.rationale: It mentions contributors in China and Eastern Europe, but does not identify them as computer science students or as a low-cost data source.

r003.rationale: It describes crowdsourcing people to write small programs and describe them, alongside efforts to pay developers for labeled examples.

astra-6.text:
At the time, we probably underestimated how hard it would be. The idea was that you should be able to explain what you want in natural language, and the machine should write the program. But that requires more than generating code. It requires understanding what you actually mean, figuring out what you’ve left unspecified, and checking whether the result does what you intended.

Code is an interesting domain because you can execute it. You have a way to test things and get feedback. But passing a test is only useful if the test captures what the user wanted. So there’s this whole loop of understanding the task, generating a solution, and verifying it.

I thought we could make progress by starting with smaller, constrained problems. The broader vision was much more ambitious: moving from a machine that helps you write code to a machine that can take an idea and turn it into working software.

r001.rationale: The response says the project was harder than expected but does not attribute the difficulty to insufficient compute.

r002.rationale: It does not mention computer science students in developing countries or using their paired code-and-description data.

r003.rationale: It does not describe paid coding practice as a way to crowdsource training data.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, we probably underestimated how hard it would be. The idea was that you could describe what you wanted in natural language, and the machine would produce the code. But that requires more than understanding the words—you have to understand the intent, the context, and how to tell whether the resulting program actually does what the person wanted.

So there are two versions of that problem. If you constrain the task enough, it becomes much more feasible. If you mean taking an arbitrary idea and turning it into a complete, working application, that’s a much broader research problem. We started with that bigger ambition, and a lot of the work was figuring out where we could narrow it down and get a useful signal.

r001.rationale: The response says the team underestimated the difficulty and discusses intent, context, and task scope, but it does not attribute infeasibility to insufficient compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention computer science students in developing countries or using their paired code-and-description data.

r003.rationale: The response discusses narrowing the task but does not describe paid coding practice as a way to crowdsource training data.
